# The Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that peculiar state of mind we spend so much energy trying to escape. It's considered a problem to solve, an enemy to defeat with endless scrolling, streaming, and distraction. But I wonder if we've gotten this completely backward.

When I was a child, boredom was a constant companion. There were whole summers where I'd exhaust every form of entertainment available and end up lying in the backyard, staring at clouds, with nothing but my own thoughts. My parents would occasionally suggest that I "find something to do," but there was a perverse relief in refusing. In those moments, something strange happened—my mind would wander into territories it never explored when actively occupied.

I'd imagine entire worlds. Not in the obsessive way of video games or books, but in this loose, associative manner where one thought would lead to another, which would somehow connect to a memory from years ago, which would spark an entirely new question I'd never considered before. I might spend an hour thinking about what it would be like if colors had sounds, or whether trees got bored, or why adults always seemed so rushed. These weren't profound philosophical insights—they were just the natural output of an idle mind given space to roam.

Now, we've essentially criminalized that state. Look around any public space and you'll see people frantically filling every gap, every moment of potential emptiness, with stimulation. We've created an entire technological ecosystem designed to make sure no one ever has to be bored again. And yet, I'm not sure we're happier. If anything, we seem more anxious, more fragmented, less capable of sustained thought or genuine creativity.

There's something important that happens in boredom that we've lost. It's not the boredom of being trapped or imprisoned—that's genuinely awful. I mean the boredom of voluntary simplicity, of choosing to do nothing in particular for a stretch of time. In those moments, the mind starts to integrate. It begins to make unexpected connections. Problems you've been consciously struggling with sometimes resolve themselves, not through effort, but through a kind of incubation that can only happen when you're not actively trying.

I think about the modern creative person, trying to work in a constant state of stimulation. They sit down to write or design or think, and there's a little notification light blinking in their periphery. Even if they resist checking it, a part of their attention remains hooked. Studies show that mere awareness of an unread notification reduces cognitive capacity. We've built our environment to be cognitively hostile to the kind of sustained, deep thinking that creates meaningful work.

And here's what's stranger: we often romanticize the conditions under which great work is done. We admire the writer's retreat, the artist's studio, the monastic scholar in his cell. What do all of these have in common? A deliberate removal from constant stimulation. A boring environment. Boring in the sense that there's not much to do but the work itself, or in the case of the monk, thinking, reading, and prayer. Yet we don't structure our own lives this way. We do the opposite.

I've noticed that boredom also has a social dimension that we've overlooked. Boredom can be a form of acceptance. When you're not trying to optimize every moment, not trying to turn every experience into content or achievement, you're actually capable of just being with another person. You can have a conversation that meanders, that doesn't accomplish anything particular, that simply exists for the pleasure of connection. When was the last time you had a conversation where neither person checked their phone? Where the silence didn't feel awkward but restful?

There's something almost radical about boredom in that sense. It says: I accept that this moment might not be optimized. I'm not trying to extract value from every second. I'm just here, and that's enough. In a culture obsessed with productivity and self-improvement, that's quietly revolutionary.

I also think about childhood differently now. Kids who are constantly overscheduled, who move from activity to activity, never experiencing that spaciousness of boredom—what are they losing? Not just creativity, though that's part of it. They're losing the experience of self-entertainment, of internal resource-building. They're not learning to be comfortable in their own minds. Every moment of potential discomfort is medicated away with structure and stimulation.

And I wonder what this costs us developmentally. Our attention spans are measurably shorter. Our ability to tolerate uncertainty is eroding. We're addicted to the certainty of algorithmic feeds, where the next thing is always calibrated to keep us interested. Real life isn't like that. Real thought isn't like that. Real growth requires periods of confusion, of not knowing what to do, of genuine boredom.

The irony is that boredom itself has become a luxury good. The wealthy, who can afford to be bored—who have the security and freedom to let time move slowly—they're often the ones producing interesting ideas and work. Meanwhile, those with less time and resources are often locked into constant stimulation, both out of necessity and because the cognitive toll of poverty and precarity doesn't leave mental energy for anything else.

I'm not suggesting we all need to go sit in empty rooms. That's not practical or even desirable for everyone. But I think we could be more intentional about creating space for boredom, for the mental wandering and integration that happens when we're not engaged in active stimulation. A walk without a podcast. A meal without checking our phones. Time in the morning before we're connected to anything.

These small acts of boredom might be among the most important things we can do for ourselves. They're where creativity lives. They're where we integrate our experiences into something coherent. They're where we remember who we are, beyond what we do, achieve, or produce.

Maybe the goal isn't to eliminate boredom, but to reclaim it as a feature of a healthy life rather than a bug to be eliminated. That seems almost impossibly countercultural now. But it might be exactly what we need.
